bib.title: The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Chapter 17: Undirected Graphical Models

question: How can the joint distribution of many variables be represented, estimated and sparsified as an undirected graph, for continuous (Gaussian) and discrete (binary) variables?
contributions: Markov graph properties (pairwise, global, cliques, Hammersley-Clifford)
Regression-based modified algorithm for fitting a Gaussian graphical model with known structure (Alg 17.1)
Ising/Boltzmann machine estimation, hidden nodes, RBMs with contrastive divergence

results.claim: RBM with 2000 hidden units, 784 visible pixels and a 10-way label unit, trained by contrastive divergence, gets 1.9% test error on MNIST.
results.source: Hinton (2002) and Hinton et al. (2006), as presented in the chapter; the chapter does not cite a specific paper for these numbers
results.setup: MNIST (LeCun et al. 1998); RBM 784 visible binary pixels + one 10-way multinomial label unit + 2000 hidden units; contrastive divergence; training set size, epochs, learning rate not given
results.quote: the RBM achieves an error rate of 1.9% on the test set

results.claim: SVM comparison error on the same MNIST task.
results.quote: 1.4% achieved by a support vector machine

results.claim: Pretraining two stacked RBMs (500 and 500 hidden units) without labels, then a 2000-hidden-unit joint RBM, reduces MNIST error to 1.25%.
results.setup: MNIST; 784 pixels replaced by 500 features from RBM(784-500) then RBM(500-500), both trained by contrastive divergence without label information; final RBM with 2000 hidden units as joint density model
results.quote: can be reduced to 1.25% by replacing the 784 pixel intensities by 500 features

limits: Authors say they do not attempt a comprehensive treatment (p.626); directed graphical models/Bayesian networks only mentioned.
Gaussian assumption is used almost always for continuous variables; non-Gaussian continuous case not treated.
Exact ML for discrete models infeasible for large p; approximations (mean field, Gibbs, contrastive divergence) discussed qualitatively.
RBM MNIST numbers given with no training details (epochs, learning rate, data split, seeds, no variance).
Choice of lambda not discussed (no cross-validation or selection rule).
Dated: 2009; deep belief nets and RBMs were later superseded by other deep learning methods; the MNIST figures are not state of the art.
practices: For continuous data, fit a Gaussian graphical model; zero entries of Theta = Sigma^-1 mark missing edges (p.630).
Estimate graph structure with the graphical lasso (L1 penalty on Theta) and examine solutions across lambda, not a single value (p.637).
When structure is known, use the coupled modified regression (Alg 17.1) rather than p separate regressions (p.633).
For binary networks with large p, use per-node L1-penalised logistic regression with min or max symmetrisation instead of exact likelihood (p.642).
Use Poisson log-linear modelling for p<20, gradient/IPF up to p about 30, mean field or Gibbs beyond (p.640-641).
Restrict to an RBM so Gibbs sampling can update whole layers at once, and use contrastive divergence (few steps from data) instead of running to stationarity (p.643-644).
Use trees (decomposable models) when closed-form ML is wanted (p.641).

terms.definition: absence of an edge implies the variables are conditionally independent given all other vertices: No edge joining X and Y <=> X ⊥ Y | rest
if C separates A and B then A ⊥ B | C
a complete subgraph, a set of vertices all adjacent to one another; maximal if no other vertex can be added and still yield a clique
positive functions psi_C over maximal cliques; f(x) = (1/Z) prod psi_C(x_C), Z is the normalizing constant, also known as the partition function
the clique-product representation implies a graph with independence properties defined by the cliques; holds for positive distributions
a potential function per edge, at most second-order interactions represented
vertices connected by bidirectional edges if the covariance (rather than partial covariance) is nonzero; negative log-likelihood not convex
maximise log det Theta - trace(S Theta) - lambda ||Theta||_1 via repeated modified lasso regressions with W11 in place of the cross-product matrix
pairwise Markov network with binary nodes, p(X,Theta)=exp[sum theta_jk X_j X_k - Phi(Theta)]
one layer of visible units and one layer of hidden units with no connections within each layer
estimate the second expectation by starting the Markov chain at the data and running only a few steps instead of to convergence
estimation of Sigma-hat as the completion of S consistent with missing edges

Chapter inconsistencies and typos: (1) p.641 mean-field text writes E(Xj)E(Xj), should be E(Xj)E(Xk). (2) p.636 footnote reference reads 'Algorithm 17.23' (meaning Algorithm 17.2, footnote 3). (3) Alg 17.1 step 3 uses s22 while Alg 17.2 uses w22 (equal by p.633, w22 = s22, and by p.636 w_jj = s_jj + lambda in glasso). (4) Fig 17.1 uses lambda = 14 but Fig 17.5 shows lambda = 0, 7, 27, 36. (5) Sec 17.3 footnote 2 calls the distribution arising from a Gaussian graphical model Wishart, which is the sampling distribution of S, loosely stated. (6) p.629 says 'subgraph U ∈ V' where subset is meant. (7) p.640 'p ≤30' vs 'larger than about 30': same threshold, consistent.
MNIST numbers are in prose only; no source cited for the 1.9%, 1.4%, 1.25% figures.
